title: CSI 2024 Dyslipidaemia Guidelines
tags: csi guideline dyslipidaemia lipid ldl statin ezetimibe a1 a4 a5
body: The Cardiological Society of India's 2024 guidance sets LDL-C targets by risk: <100 mg/dL low/moderate, <70 high, <55 for established ASCVD, <40 for recurrent events. For ACS and very-high-risk patients it directs a high-intensity statin PLUS ezetimibe upfront rather than statin monotherapy first. Escalation at 4 weeks runs to bempedoic acid, then PCSK9 inhibitors. This is what turns statin combinations from a second-line add-on into first-line therapy, and it is the single biggest driver behind A1 and A4.
source: Indian Heart Journal 2024;76(S1):S6-S19; csi.org.in

title: IHCI hypertension treatment protocol
tags: ihci hypertension protocol step telmisartan amlodipine chlorthalidone a7 a8 a9
body: The India Hypertension Control Initiative standard protocol runs: Step 1 amlodipine 5mg (or telmisartan 40mg for diabetics); Step 2 escalate or add a second agent to form a dual; Step 3 amlodipine + telmisartan 80mg + chlorthalidone 12.5mg as a triple. Delivered through Health & Wellness Centres with 30-day refills. This protocol is why A7 exists as a growing tier, and it is the reason a telmisartan-backbone triple is guideline-backed rather than a commercial invention — which matters directly for CDSCO ban risk.
source: ihci.in standard treatment protocol; WHO India HEARTS

title: ESC 2024 and the single-pill combination shift
tags: esc single pill combination spc monotherapy adherence a7 a8 a9
body: ESC 2024 carries a Class I recommendation to initiate most hypertensive patients on a two-drug single-pill combination rather than monotherapy, reserving monotherapy for low-risk grade 1, the very elderly and the frail. Indian trial data (TOPSPIN, 32+ sites) shows roughly 70% BP control on dual single-pill combinations against under 45% for monotherapy escalation. This is why A9 first-line monotherapy is a hold-not-invest call: guidelines are moving patients out of it, not into it.
source: ESC 2024 Hypertension Guidelines, escardio.org; TOPSPIN trial, IJMR

title: CDSCO fixed-dose combination bans
tags: cdsco fdc ban regulatory risk irrational combination
body: CDSCO banned 156 irrational FDCs in August 2024 and a further 16 in June 2026. Both waves targeted combinations without a clinical rationale, not combinations as a category. Guideline-backed combinations were not affected. This is the core of our regulatory answer: every combination in our plan is guideline-endorsed — the telmisartan triple is the IHCI Step-3 protocol, and statin + ezetimibe is CSI 2024's upfront recommendation for ACS. We are not betting on a combination that exists only because it sells.
source: CDSCO FDC ban notices, Aug 2024 and Jun 2026; PIB

title: NLEM 2022 price control and why FDCs protect margin
tags: nlem nppa dpco price cap ceiling margin realisation
body: NLEM 2022 / DPCO ceilings cap plain atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, amlodipine, telmisartan, losartan, aspirin 75/150 and clopidogrel 75 — precisely the molecules that make up Cipla's existing cardiac base. Strategic FDCs generally sit outside the strict ceilings. So moving weight from plain molecules and step-up duals onto guideline-backed triples protects realisation as well as share. The price-cap squeeze is an argument FOR the shift, not against it.
source: NPPA nppaindia.gov.in; NLEM 2022 gazette; DPCO 2013

title: Cipla strategy leadership on winning as a challenger
tags: challenger whitespace mindshare share of voice doctors universe five lakh strategy head guidance how to win entering therapy area
body: PRIMARY GUIDANCE from Cipla's strategy leadership, mentoring session 26 Aug 2026 — this is what the people judging us said matters. Entering a large therapy area is not itself the bet; finding the right whitespace and executing against it is. Because India is a branded-generics market, doctor mindshare and share of voice are the currency. The instruction is explicit: identify the RELEVANT doctors rather than trying to cover the universe, which is roughly 5 lakh doctors in India. Beyond that, what separates a bet that pays off is access to a differentiated product, a strong patient proposition, and the ability to identify unmet needs in patient education and counselling. Hospital channels matter depending on therapy. The bet works when product, doctors, patient value and focused execution line up together.

title: Build vs buy — leadership favours partnership and licensing as accelerators
tags: build buy m&a acquisition licensing partnership mnc organic capability speed torrent jb chem why not acquire
body: PRIMARY GUIDANCE, same session. Partnerships, licensing and M&A are seen as legitimate and important ways to accelerate capability building, not fallbacks. Cipla's standing as a preferred MNC partner gives it access to products and capabilities through licensing. The stated test is how quickly and effectively the required capability can be acquired — there is NO automatic preference for building organically. This matters for us: our plan builds a specialist force from scratch, and we should be able to say why building beats licensing HERE specifically, rather than assuming organic is the default. The honest answer is that the molecules already exist and are already registered to many companies, so there is nothing to in-license — the missing asset is prescriber relationships, which cannot be bought except by acquiring a company that has them.
source: Cipla strategy leadership, Ascend S4 mentoring session, 26 Aug 2026

title: FDC regulatory risk — guideline backing alone is not the answer
tags: fdc regulatory dcgi approval ban risk medical rationale evidence drug interaction clinical trial cdsco sustainable multi-year
body: PRIMARY GUIDANCE, same session, and it raises our bar. Regulatory uncertainty must be built into the product decision from the beginning, not handled afterwards. The specific considerations named were: regulatory strategy, DCGI approval, medical rationale for the combination, evidence on drug-drug interactions, and clinical-trial evidence. The explicit risk flagged was launching WITHOUT appropriate DCGI approval and then facing a ban. Our current answer — that the telmisartan triple is IHCI Step-3 and therefore guideline-backed — is necessary but not sufficient. We should state DCGI approval status directly. Supporting fact from the dataset: the cilnidipine-chlorthalidone-telmisartan triple is already marketed by 54 companies and the metoprolol triple by 21, which implies existing approvals rather than a fresh filing — but say that as an inference, and confirm it rather than assert it.
source: Cipla strategy leadership, Ascend S4 mentoring session, 26 Aug 2026

title: What actually wins the internal investment case
tags: internal competition respiratory us generics budget business case differentiation dosing convenience patient consumer doctor customer why fund cardiac
body: PRIMARY GUIDANCE, same session — and it says our current argument is the wrong one. The case for investment rests on the QUALITY of the opportunity, not the current size of the business. What was named specifically: differentiation through pricing, through dosing and convenience, and through positioning. In a branded-generic market a differentiated product can create value even when the molecule is not unique. A crucial distinction was drawn between the DOCTOR as customer and prescriber, and the PATIENT as consumer. The cardiac case gets stronger when it offers a differentiated proposition, better convenience or dosing, a meaningful patient benefit, and a long-term franchise. Our deck argues mostly on pool size and growth rate. Our strongest unused card is convenience: one pill instead of three, which is an adherence argument and therefore a patient benefit, not just a commercial one.
source: Cipla strategy leadership, Ascend S4 mentoring session, 26 Aug 2026

title: Field force — redeployment is harder than our plan assumes
tags: field force reallocation redeploy new team dedicated 70 reps retraining friction one india gtm organizational geographic segmentation gorakhpur vellore
body: PRIMARY GUIDANCE, same session, and it corrects a load-bearing assumption. Simply shifting representatives from one therapy to another is not straightforward: the organisation has to ask whether the target doctors and patient segmentation are genuinely different. In practice Cipla has created NEW dedicated teams rather than redeploying — a precedent of 70+ representatives was cited, including specific deployment towards cardio. That is real validation that our ~110-rep figure is the right order of magnitude, but it means the force should be costed as a NEW team rather than as weight reallocated off A8. A 12-month roadmap must account for therapy expertise, retraining time, doctor and segment overlap, and whether a dedicated team beats redeployment. Leadership also stressed hospital-level and GEOGRAPHIC segmentation — naming migrant-population markets such as Gorakhpur and Vellore — and said GTM cannot be designed purely at an all-India level. That directly supports our state-level launch sequencing.
source: Cipla strategy leadership, Ascend S4 mentoring session, 26 Aug 2026

title: The stockist network is an enabler, not an advantage
tags: stockist network distribution reach tier 2 3 channel margin inventory pull prescription adoption advantage 5500
body: PRIMARY GUIDANCE, same session, and it softens a claim we lean on. Asked directly about channel-margin or inventory friction in scaling high-value dual and triple combinations, leadership identified no specific stockist constraint — but redirected to the point that matters: reach by itself does not guarantee adoption. For chronic therapy the opportunity is tied to sustained prescriptions and patient consumption rather than one-time demand, so scaling depends on prescription strength, product differentiation, pricing, relevant doctor coverage, hospital access, and patient adherence. The 5,500+ stockist network provides reach; the commercial proposition has to pull product through it. Our deck treats the network as a competitive advantage for Tier 2-3 — the honest framing is that it removes a barrier competitors would face, but it does not generate demand.
source: Cipla strategy leadership, Ascend S4 mentoring session, 26 Aug 2026

title: Launches from zero do not work — Cipla's own record proves it
tags: launch launches lead with a launch why not a launch launch-led risk standing start new molecule entry precedent can we launch rosulip ez
body: Computed from the case dataset. Cipla launched SEVEN products into cardiac between MAT Feb'24 and Feb'26. Together they total Rs 1.94 Cr. The best was ROSULIP EZ at Rs 0.99 Cr. Into the chlorthalidone+cilnidipine+telmisartan launch molecule specifically, 13 companies entered from zero in the window and all thirteen together reached Rs 1.9 Cr — 0.8% of a Rs 249 Cr pool; the best single one was Fidus Healthcare at Rs 0.94 Cr. Across all 279 companies, the best standing start into ANY addressable A7 molecule in two years was Torrent at Rs 3.92 Cr (1.87% of pool), one success in 55 attempts. So an assumption that a new launch delivers Rs 15 Cr is 15x Cipla's own best launch and 4x the best anyone achieved in A7. We therefore size the launch at Rs 5 Cr and make it a Horizon 2 addition, not the Horizon 1 headline — the Rs 35 Cr comes from converting Cipla's own patients onto triples Cipla already sells. ROSULIP EZ is also the best proof of the whole thesis: Cipla launched into the fastest-growing molecule in the dataset (ezetimibe+rosuvastatin, Rs 183 Cr pool growing +91.5% value on +77.4% volume, 33 companies, USV 21.1% and Emcure 19.6% leading) and holds 0.54% two years later. The portfolio is not the problem. NOTE the deck's A1 slide once said 'launch a Rosuvastatin + Ezetimibe FDC' — Cipla already launched it. It is a scale-up, not a launch.

title: Cipla's own duals are the acquisition engine, and it can already make the triple
tags: cannibalisation conversion feeder dual step up targeting prescriber a8 healthy harvest declining losing retention manufacture make triple amlopres cresar metolar
body: CAN CIPLA MAKE IT: the launch triple (chlorthalidone + cilnidipine + telmisartan) is the merge of two duals Cipla already manufactures — CILOGARD T / CRESAR LN (cilnidipine+telmisartan, Rs 1.95 Cr, +14.3% volume) and CRESAR CT / TECHLOR (chlorthalidone+telmisartan, Rs 4.48 Cr) — on a telmisartan franchise worth Rs 90.7 Cr across 15 molecules. It is a line extension, not new chemistry. THE FEEDER MAP: Cipla's telmisartan duals are the patients who fail on two drugs and need a third. AMLOPRES-TL + CRESAR-AM (amlodipine+telmisartan) Rs 46.9 Cr at -6.0% volume step into AMLOPRES TRIO and CRESAR AMH; METOLAR TL Rs 7.5 Cr at -10.7% steps into METOLAR TRIO; CRESAR-H Rs 8.6 Cr at -12.4% steps into CRESAR AMH; CRESAR CT and CILOGARD T step into the launch triple. Total telmisartan-dual base Rs 69.4 Cr across those four named brands, Rs 71.0 Cr counting every Cipla telmisartan dual. IMPORTANT RETRACTION - DO NOT CLAIM THE FEEDER BASE AS AN ADVANTAGE. An earlier version of this deck said no rival entering these molecules has Cipla's targeting list. That is wrong. Cipla ranks 18th of 175 companies in telmisartan duals; Mankind holds Rs 517.8 Cr, seven times more, and Glenmark Rs 1,140 Cr, sixteen times more. Cipla does know which doctors write its own duals, but so does every rival with a bigger base, so it is not a differentiator. The defensible claim is CONVERSION RATE, not base size - see [[differentiation]] and [[shrinking-base]]. CORRECTION TO THE DECK: it names AMLOPRES-AT (Rs 96.2 Cr) as the main cannibalisation exposure, but AMLOPRES-AT is amlodipine + ATENOLOL, not a telmisartan dual, so it does not step up into a telmisartan triple. A8 REFRAME: Cipla's A8 volume is -4.3% while the A8 market is +2.2%. Cipla is already losing A8 patients; the +2.5% revenue line is price and mix covering it. So the triple is not cannibalising a healthy franchise, it is the retention vehicle for one that is already leaking. Nobody is asked to give up revenue — that is the internal case.

title: How the case Excel is used, and what it says that the deck does not

body: The file has two sheets (Glossary, Cardiac) and 36 columns over 7,452 rows. Our engine reads all 7,452 rows, all 279 companies, 285 molecules and 3,788 brands, and uses 13 columns: MOLECULE_DESC, BRANDS, COMPANY, SUBGROUP, the three MAT value series, MAT CP Feb'24 and Feb'26, QTY MAT Feb'24 and Feb'26, and the three monthly sales columns. Most unused columns are genuinely empty of signal — SUPERGROUP and ACUTE_CHRONIC have one value each, FINAL NFC is 99.4% SOLIDS, PACK VOLUME is blank on 7,412 of 7,452 rows. FOUR unused columns do carry signal. (1) THE TAXONOMY WE WERE GIVEN: CARDIAC SUB SEGMENTS has 15 values. Crosswalked against our nine archetypes: A7 IS 'AHT Triple / Poly Comb.' 100% — Rs 1,472 Cr against their Rs 1,473 Cr, effectively identical, so our archetype reproduces their segment exactly. But their single 'Statins Comb.' segment, Rs 4,154 Cr, splits across our A1 (70% of it), A3 (22%) and A4 (8%), and their four drug-class segments CCB, ARBs, ACEi and Alfa Blockers, Rs 4,824 Cr together, all land inside our A9. So our taxonomy reproduces theirs where theirs tracks clinical use and splits it where it does not — that is the answer to 'why did you build your own segmentation'. (2) MANUFACT. DESC: Cipla manufactures 137 of its 137 cardiac SKUs in-house, 100% of value. Inside the A7 triples only 83% of value is self-manufactured — 56 of 552 SKUs are third-party or loan-licensed (56 of 552 SKUs). Cipla is a manufacturer in a segment where a slice of the competition is not. (3) INDIAN_MNC: MNCs are Rs 1,110 Cr of Rs 23,244 Cr, 4.8%. Indian cardiac is an all-Indian fight; no MNC is a competitive threat here. (4) Plain/Combination: combinations are Rs 13,477 Cr against Rs 9,767 Cr plain — 58% of the market is already FDC, which validates the archetype classifier independently.

title: Who loses if this plan works — the displacement test
tags: competitor response competitors retaliate retaliation defend defence who loses displacement take share zero sum rivals react mankind aristo macleods glenmark what will competitors do fight back
body: Asked what competitors will do, or who loses, use this. The plan does NOT require Cipla to take absolute revenue off any rival. Over the 36-month build, the A1 pool grows by Rs 953 Cr on its own and the A7 pool by Rs 741 Cr — Rs 1,694 Cr of new money between them. Cipla's entire build is Rs 123.5 Cr, which is 7.3% of that growth (A1 6.6%, A7 8.2%). So every competitor can keep growing in absolute rupees while this plan runs. In share terms Cipla moves 0.79% to 2.55% in A1 and 0.71% to 3.51% in A7 — 1.76 and 2.80 share points, spread across 120 and 107 companies respectively. No single rival wakes up to a loss worth mounting a defence against, which is also the best explanation for why this gap has stayed open. THE SECOND HALF OF THE ANSWER: the patients Cipla converts are its OWN — it moves its own dual-therapy patients up to its own triple. It is not prospecting in someone else's prescriber base. STATE THE LIMIT HONESTLY IF PUSHED: this is a check ON the plan, computed after the two spaces were chosen. It did not drive the selection, and we do not model how a rival would respond if it did decide to contest.
source: Computed by underwrite() displacement test; pool growth at each space's own CAGR over the 36-month build

title: Why there is no A2 — the one archetype that holds nothing
tags: a2 antiplatelet antiplatelets aspirin clopidogrel ticagrelor prasugrel monotherapy missing empty absent gap why no a2 skipped numbering b01 antithrombotic scope taxonomy
body: A2 Antiplatelet-led Prevention is defined in our taxonomy and holds ZERO SKUs. The reason is the dataset's scope, not anything about the Indian market. The case file carries 14 drug groups and every one is C01, C02 or C10 — cardiac therapy, antihypertensives, lipid modifiers. There is no B01 antithrombotic group, and none of the 15 CARDIAC SUB SEGMENTS is an antiplatelet category. Searched across molecule name AND subgroup text for every spelling (aspirin, asprin, ASA, acetylsalicylic, clopidogrel, clopidgrl, clopid, ticagrelor, prasugrel), 837 SKUs worth Rs 2,894 Cr mention an antiplatelet and NOT ONE of them is a single molecule — all 22 distinct antiplatelet molecules in the file are combinations. Plain aspirin, plain clopidogrel, ticagrelor and prasugrel return zero rows. So every antiplatelet in this data is an INGREDIENT inside a statin combination, filed under C10A STATINS / 'Statins Comb.', which our classifier routes to A1 Secondary Prevention. A2 could never populate, because the products that would fill it are outside the file. DO NOT SAY the empty A2 shows that antiplatelet monotherapy has been absorbed into fixed-dose combinations, or that it validates the FDC shift. That is a claim about the market, and this dataset cannot support it either way — the category is missing from the data, which tells you nothing about prescribing. The correct answer is a scope statement: we cannot size antiplatelet monotherapy from this file, and every antiplatelet we can see is already inside a combination. Implementation note if anyone reads the code: the ANTIPLATELET pattern keys on 'ASPIRIN' rather than 'ACETYLSALICYLIC', and works because IQVIA's SUBGROUP codes spell it out (C10A0A ATORVA + ASPIRIN). 832 of the 837 land in A1. The other 5 are Rs 4.15 Cr of aspirin polypills and aspirin+nitrate; Rs 4.15 Cr of that sits in a locked molecule and Rs 0.00 Cr is addressable, so no published pool moves by a rupee.
source: Case dataset column and molecule audit, verified 2 Sep 2026

title: Year-on-year, not two-year average — what is accelerating and what is fading
tags: acceleration fading momentum year on year feb25 midpoint recent trend is growth slowing
body: Every growth figure in the deck is a two-year CAGR from MAT Feb'24 to Feb'26, which treats 100->180->200 and 100->110->200 identically. Splitting on the Feb'25 midpoint (units, year-on-year): ACCELERATING — the launch triple pool 13.3% to 17.7%; A7 as a whole 10.7% to 12.9%; the Amlopres Trio pool 4.2% to 9.6%; the Metolar Trio tartrate pool 44.9% to 47.1%; and critically ROSULIP-CV, where Cipla's own units went 7.8% to 17.0%. FADING — and this must be volunteered, not hidden: Cipla's own momentum in BOTH A7 focus brands is decelerating sharply. CRESAR AMH units 38.5% to 4.0%; METOLAR TRIO units 129.7% to 38.9%. The two-year averages quoted for those brands conceal a slowdown in the most recent year, and the contrast is the point: Cresar AMH's own pool went 7.0% to 9.2% and Metolar Trio's pools 29.4% to 30.8% while the Cipla brands inside them decelerated. The honest reading is that both brands got an initial burst and then flattened — which is exactly what happens to a product with no sustained detailing behind it, and is therefore an argument FOR the task force rather than against the picks. But a judge can compute it, so say it first. STEADY — Rosulip-ASP pool, Atorlip-CV pool (5.1% to 4.1%, supporting its 2% weighting), the Rosuvastatin+Ezetimibe pool holding 77.7% then 77.2% unit growth, and Cipla's total cardiac at -4.2% then -3.7% units against a market at 2.2% then 5.1%, i.e. still shrinking.

title: The five personas — three customers, two consumers
tags: persona personas how many personas customer consumer doctor patient prescriber buyer payer patient persona ramesh sunita dr rao dr iyer dr sharma who is the patient adherence persistence epidemiology india prevalence nfhs indiab pure cascade resistant hypertension secondary prevention why do patients stop
body: THE FRAMING THAT ORGANISES THEM, and it came from the strategy head: in this market the DOCTOR IS THE CUSTOMER and the PATIENT IS THE CONSUMER. They are not the same person. The doctor decides; the patient pays and swallows. A plan that persuades only one of them fails, which is why there are five personas and not two. THE CUSTOMERS - three doctors, each a different buyer. DR. RAO, interventional cardiologist, about 5,000 in India, decides the post-ACS discharge regimen, moved by CSI 2024 outcome data and KOL peers, reached by high-science detailing: 50 reps. DR. IYER, consulting physician, about 15,000 high-decile, decides whether to add a third drug, moved by the IHCI Step-3 protocol which already names the triple and covers 141 districts and 303 million people, lifting BP control from 37% to 48%: 60 reps. DR. SHARMA, Tier-2/3 GP, the long tail, decides whether the prescription gets substituted at refill, moved by availability and shelf price, reached by the existing 5,500-stockist network: ZERO new reps. Sharma matters and still gets no headcount - winning him is a stocking job, not a detailing job, and that is precisely why the task force is 110 people rather than 300. THE CONSUMERS - two patients. RAMESH KULKARNI, 54, Nashik shopkeeper, the A7 patient. He is one of roughly 315 million Indian adults with hypertension — 35.5% of everyone over 20 (ICMR-INDIAB-17, Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, Jul 2023). NFHS-5 puts the care cascade at 70.5% ever screened, 34.3% aware, 13.7% on treatment, 7.8% controlled: Ramesh is inside the 13.7% and outside the 7.8%. On two drugs he is still 158/96, which places him in the 10-16% of treated Indian hypertensives who resist dual therapy. He takes three separate pills at three times of day; 32.7% of rural south Indian NCD patients are non-adherent and 78.6% say the medicines are hard to pay for. What fixes it is the third drug in the same pill — single-pill combinations roughly double persistence against the same molecules taken separately (meta-analysis, 27 studies, 346,030 patients). He is already on Amlopres-TL, a Cipla dual inside the Rs 69.4 Cr that is leaking at about 6% a year. His next prescription is Cresar AMH or it is Mankind's. SUNITA MENON, 56, Kochi school administrator, the A1 patient. Stented 14 months ago. The mean age of a first MI in India is about 53, roughly a decade earlier than Western populations, and 52% of India's CVD deaths occur under 50. She was discharged on four drugs and is on one. PURE found only 23.6% of people with established CVD on an antiplatelet and 15.5% on a statin; in India use peaked at 43% and fell back to 21.6%. Rural statin use is 11.6% against 19.9% urban. What fixes it is her discharge regimen collapsed into one tablet — rosuvastatin + clopidogrel, which is exactly Rosulip-CV, where Cipla holds 0.89% of a Rs 323 Cr pool. THE POINT: neither persona requires Cipla to find a new patient. Both are already on a Cipla prescription, written by a doctor Cipla can already reach; the only question is whether the next one is also Cipla's. THE CONSUMER IS ALSO THE PAYER, which is the opening nobody is using. Under IHCI's public-channel programme, patients' out-of-pocket medicine cost fell from 47% to 9%. In the private channel, where Cipla sells, it is unsolved - 78.6% of Indian patients on cardiovascular medicines say they are hard to pay for. One pill instead of three is a cost argument and an adherence argument in the same sentence. The prescribers are Dr. Rao (interventional cardiologist, ~5,000 in India, sees Sunita at discharge) and Dr. Iyer (consulting physician, ~15,000 high-decile, sees Ramesh, moved by the IHCI Step-3 protocol which now covers 141 districts and 303 million people and lifted BP control from 37% to 48%).
source: ICMR-INDIAB 2023; NFHS-5 2019-21; PURE (Lancet 2011, JACC 2024); CREATE registry; IHCI/BMC HSR 2024; SPC adherence meta-analysis 2023

title: The differentiation — conversion rate, not base size (and the claim we had to retract)
tags: differentiation why cipla not mankind what is your edge moat right to win conversion ratio feeder base defensible advantage air quality pm2.5 pollution
body: We first assumed Cipla's edge in A7 was owning the feeder patients. The data says no. Cipla ranks 18th of 175 companies in telmisartan duals with Rs 71.0 Cr. Mankind holds Rs 517.8 Cr, seven times more; Glenmark holds Rs 1,140 Cr, sixteen times more. On base size Cipla loses, so base size is not the argument. What separates companies here is CONVERSION: A7 triples divided by telmisartan-dual base. Micro Labs 0.96, Macleods 0.96, Sun 0.69, IPCA 0.48, Lupin 0.39, Aristo 0.38, Intas 0.37, Eris 0.36, Mankind 0.25, Torrent 0.22, USV 0.19, CIPLA 0.14, Glenmark 0.07. Median across the 20 companies with a Rs 50 Cr+ base is 0.27. Cipla ranks 17th of 20. THE CLAIM: Cipla's advantage is not that it has the most patients, it is that it converts the fewest of the ones it has — so every rupee of the plan needs no new patient and no competitive win, only that Cipla convert its own dual patients at a rate its peers already reach. The Rs 35 Cr target implies a ratio of 0.62, above the median and below Sun. This is an INDEPENDENT second check on the number: the IPCA share-multiple anchor and the conversion-ratio anchor were computed separately and land in the same place. WHY HASN'T SOMEONE DONE IT: Glenmark has the largest dual base in the market and converts 7% of it. A feeder base converts nothing on its own; it takes a team pointed at it. Also note the step-up is already happening unaided inside Cipla's own franchises — Cresar duals -11.1% units last year while Cresar triples +17.9%; Metolar duals -7.7% while Metolar triples +41.7%. Same reps, same doctors, same brand name. CAVEAT TO VOLUNTEER: Cipla's dual base is itself shrinking at 10.6% units a year, so the window narrows — an argument for moving now, not later. WHAT IS NOT A DIFFERENTIATOR: in-house manufacturing. Cipla makes 137 of 137 cardiac SKUs itself, but so do Mankind, Aristo, Macleods and IPCA, all at 100%. It is table stakes. It is only notable that Sun, the largest A7 player at Rs 139 Cr, self-manufactures none of its A7 SKUs, and Torrent only 43%. EXTERNAL TAILWIND SPECIFIC TO A7: PM2.5. Hypertension prevalence in India rises 5.2% per 10 ug/m3 of PM2.5 (Int J Epidemiology 2025); a Delhi cohort links long-term exposure to higher systolic BP and incident hypertension (Hypertension/AHA 2020). Meeting the National Clean Air Programme target would cut prevalence only 2.42%, so the exposure persists across the 3-5 year window. It enlarges the share of patients not controlled on two drugs, which is the definition of A7 — the only signal in our register that acts on one archetype rather than the whole category.
source: Case dataset conversion analysis 27 Aug 2026; Int J Epidemiology 2025; Hypertension (AHA) 2020

title: Price test — the alternative explanation for low conversion, and why it fails
tags: price pricing priced out too expensive cheaper cost per tablet realisation is price the problem alternative explanation rebuttal glenmark
body: The obvious rival explanation for Cipla's low conversion is price: maybe Cipla simply costs more and doctors switch on cost. We tested it by computing realised price per tablet (MAT Feb'26 value divided by MAT quantity; note QTY in this dataset is in THOUSANDS of units, so the market average works out to Rs 8.07 a tablet). Results across the five focus molecules, Cipla versus the molecule's weighted-average price: Rosuvastatin+Clopidogrel +9.0% (Cipla 0.69% share; Lupin at +42.9% holds 20.2%); ASA+Rosuvastatin -4.2% (Cipla 0.88%; Torrent at +21.3% holds 31.9%); Atorvastatin+Clopidogrel -0.8% (Cipla 0.54%; Ajanta at +13.8% holds 16.8%); Cilnidipine+Metoprolol+Telmisartan -8.0% (Cipla 1.13%; Ajanta at +13.5% holds 23.2%); Amlodipine+HCTZ+Telmisartan +84.5% (Cipla 1.11%). CONCLUSION: in four of the five molecules Cipla is at or BELOW market price and still holds under 1.2% share. Cheaper products are losing to dearer ones by as much as 36x, so this market does not clear on price. The fifth molecule is the only one where Cipla really is expensive - and there the decisive comparison is GLENMARK, which prices within 1% of Cipla (Rs 16,853 vs Rs 16,700 per thousand tablets) and holds Rs 57.6 Cr against Cipla's Rs 5.2 Cr, eleven times more at the same price. Price cannot explain an 11x gap between two products priced identically. The detailing thesis survives the test. CAVEAT to volunteer: price per tablet does not adjust for strength mix, so treat the percentages as a range rather than a decimal; the Glenmark comparison is same-molecule and same-price, which is why it is the one to lead with. SECONDARY READ: premium pricing is viable in these molecules - Lupin, Torrent, Ajanta and Glenmark all run above market and hold large shares. So the recommendation is NOT to cut price. It is that Cipla currently charges premium prices with no field effort behind them, which is the worst of both positions.
source: Case dataset price analysis, 27 Aug 2026

title: The shrinking feeder base — propagated through the model, not just flagged
tags: shrinking base feeder declining denominator does the target survive sensitivity share loss category decline mankind taking share window narrowing
body: Cipla's telmisartan-dual base is Rs 71.0 Cr and falling 10.6% in units year on year, so the Rs 35 Cr A7 gain cannot rest on today's base indefinitely. Two findings. FIRST, THE REASON: this is share loss, not category decline. The telmisartan-dual market grew units +6.4% then +7.4% and value +13.7% then +14.9% to Rs 4,950 Cr. Mankind's slice grew units +8.8% then +8.2% to Rs 517.8 Cr. Only Cipla's slice fell - units +0.3% then -10.6%, value +9.5% then -3.5%. So delay does not merely shrink the prize, it transfers the feeder patients to Mankind permanently. SECOND, DOES THE TARGET SURVIVE: the Rs 44.1 Cr year-5 A7 figure implies a conversion ratio of 0.62 on today's Rs 71.0 Cr base. Projected five years: if last year's decline repeats (-3.5% value a year) the base is Rs 59 Cr and the implied ratio 0.74, between Sun (0.69) and Macleods (0.96); on the 2-year value CAGR (+2.8%) the base is Rs 82 Cr and the ratio 0.54, between IPCA (0.48) and Sun; if Cipla merely stops losing share the base holds at Rs 71 Cr and the ratio is 0.62. Even the worst case stays inside observed behaviour - it asks Cipla to convert slightly better than Sun, third best of the twenty companies with a Rs 50 Cr+ base. Demanding, not unprecedented. TWO CAVEATS TO VOLUNTEER: (1) converting a patient shrinks the base the ratio is measured against, so the ratio partly inflates itself - the rupee figure is the commitment and the ratio is the diagnostic, not a target to maximise; (2) the shrinkage is self-limiting under the plan, because the patients leaving are precisely the ones the plan retains.
source: Case dataset, feeder-base projection 27 Aug 2026

title: A8 and A5 are both feeders — the symmetry the engine found on its own
tags: a5 a8 a3 a6 a9 feeder is a5 a feeder plain statin base primary lipid convert harvest avoid defend a3 worth funding two feeders symmetry sixty four percent of book strategic calls double down build selective avoid classifier
body: The deck's four strategic calls are: DOUBLE DOWN on A7 and A1; CONVERT A8 and A5; DEFEND A3 without funding growth; AVOID further investment in A6 and A9. The CONVERT call covers TWO archetypes, not one. A8 Step-up Dual is Rs 184.6 Cr of Cipla's book with units at -4.3% against an A8 market at +2.2%. A5 Primary Lipid is Rs 64.5 Cr with units at -1.6% against an A5 market at +5.3%. Together they are Rs 249.1 Cr, 64% of Cipla's Rs 389 Cr cardiac book, and BOTH are leaking. THE SYMMETRY: A8 is the feeder for A7 (telmisartan duals stepping up to triples, Cipla converts 0.14 against a 0.27 median) and A5 is the feeder for A1 (plain statins stepping up to combinations, Cipla converts 0.29 against a 0.59 median). Two feeders, two destinations, the same defect in both - so this is one problem with one fix, not two separate initiatives. See [[differentiation]]. An earlier version of the deck put A5 under AVOID. That was wrong and inconsistent with our own A1 conversion analysis; A5 is the A1 feeder and is corrected to CONVERT. THE ENGINE DERIVES THIS ITSELF: the classifier rule is that a space Cipla holds above 2% share, where Cipla's own units are negative AND below the market's, is not a harvest but a leak - 'CONVERT - leaking, redirect patients'. Run rank_opportunities live and it returns CONVERT for A8 and A5 without being told to.
source: Case dataset; cipla_cardiac_agent.py classifier, 27 Aug 2026

title: A4 — the one call where our model and our judgement differ, and we say so
tags: a4 intensive lipid ezetimibe why not a4 horizon 3 excluded score 69 second highest flat pool rosulip ez disagree with the model
body: Our agent scores A4 Intensive Lipid 69.1, the SECOND HIGHEST of the nine archetypes, because it grows 55.8% a year and its leader holds only 15.3%. Its computed prize is nonetheless only Rs 19 Cr. Both are true and the gap is a method choice, not an error: our sizing holds every pool flat at MAT Feb'26 size and treats pool growth as uncounted upside, which penalises the fastest-growing space hardest. Sized on a grown pool the picture changes - at the engine's projected 41.7% CAGR A4 is about Rs 114 Cr, at a conservative 30% about Rs 74 Cr, at a very conservative 20% about Rs 49 Cr, larger than A7's underwritten Rs 35 Cr. IMPORTANT: growing A4's pool without growing the others is not a fair comparison. Grow every pool at its own projected rate and the order is A1 Rs 220 Cr, A7 Rs 132 Cr, A4 Rs 114 Cr - so the PRIORITY ORDER SURVIVES either way, which is the real point. A7 and A1 still lead. A4 moves from smallest on the board to roughly A7's size. OUR DECISION: A4 stays outside the underwritten Rs 62 Cr, deliberately, because the flat-pool convention is what makes Rs 62 Cr conservative and defensible, and we will not relax it for one archetype. Cipla is not a standing start there - ROSULIP EZ is already on the shelf at 0.54% of a Rs 183 Cr pool growing 91.5% in value. NEVER SAY A4 IS UNATTRACTIVE. It is the fastest-growing space in the dataset and our own model ranks it second. Say instead that it is an exclusion we chose rather than one the data forced, and that Rs 61 Cr - a figure an earlier draft carried - was wrong; the engine computes Rs 19 Cr on a flat pool.
source: Case dataset; rank_opportunities and project_forward, 27 Aug 2026

title: The recommendation in full — the whole answer in one place
tags: recommendation final solution answer summary what should cipla do the plan overall bottom line in one minute whole answer wrap up conclusion so what
body: THE FOUR CALLS. DOUBLE DOWN on A7 Resistant Hypertension and A1 Secondary Prevention. CONVERT A8 Step-up Dual and A5 Primary Lipid - Cipla's two big leaking feeder franchises, Rs 249 Cr and 64% of its cardiac book, which feed A7 and A1 respectively. DEFEND A3 Cardiometabolic without funding growth. AVOID further investment in A6 and A9. A4 Intensive Lipid is a DELIBERATE EXCLUSION, not an oversight - see [[a4-exclusion]]. THE MONEY, AND THE ARITHMETIC MUST BE STATED CAREFULLY. A7 contributes Rs 35 Cr and A1 Rs 38 Cr, which is Rs 73 Cr GROSS. From that we deduct about Rs 11 Cr of Cipla's own leaking dual patients converting into the focus triples, giving Rs 62 Cr NET. DO NOT say Rs 62 Cr is Rs 35 Cr plus Rs 38 Cr - that sum is Rs 73 Cr, and the Rs 62 Cr is what survives cannibalisation. The Rs 62 Cr takes Cipla's cardiac book from Rs 389 Cr to Rs 451 Cr over five years. Modelled headroom is Rs 201 Cr; we underwrite 31% of it, and break even at 16%. WHAT IS ACTUALLY DONE. Not a launch. Detail four brands Cipla already sells: CRESAR AMH and METOLAR TRIO in A7, ROSULIP-CV and ROSULIP-ASP in A1, with ATORLIP-CV funded at a deliberate 2% because Cipla is losing 14.8% of its units there each year. Consolidate Amlopres Trio and Cresar Plus onto Cresar AMH in month one - three Cipla brands sit on one molecule, so this doubles detailing weight at no cost. The new triple (chlortalidone + cilnidipine + telmisartan) moves to Horizon 2 carrying Rs 5 Cr, not Rs 15 Cr, because launches from a standing start do not scale - see [[launch-precedent]]. WHAT HAS TO BE BUILT. A Cardio-Metabolic Task Force of about 110 reps: 50 against roughly 5,000 cardiologists, 60 against roughly 15,000 high-decile physicians, none against Tier-2/3 GPs, who are served by the existing stockist network. Rs 4-5 Cr in the pilot year, Rs 15-19 Cr a year at full scale, funded from A8's budget rather than A8's reps. Pay on 90-day repeat chemist offtake, the closest thing to persistence that is measurable monthly. See [[taskforce]]. WHY IT IS DEFENSIBLE. The differentiation is conversion rate, not base size - Cipla converts 0.14 of its telmisartan-dual base into triples against a 0.27 median, and 0.29 of its plain-statin base into A1 combinations against a 0.59 median. Half the median in both funded archetypes. Every rupee needs no new patient and no competitive win. See [[differentiation]] and [[feeder-symmetry]]. THE PATIENTS. Ramesh Kulkarni, 54, uncontrolled on two drugs; Sunita Menon, 56, stented and down to one of four discharge medicines. Both are already on a Cipla prescription - see [[patient-personas]].
source: Team JK synthesis of the case dataset analysis, 27 Aug 2026

title: BCG and Ansoff applied — one diagnoses the past, the other describes the plan
tags: frameworks what frameworks did you use which framework bcg matrix ansoff framework star cash cow dog question mark market penetration product development diversification relative share classical lens strategy framework hr sfe build buy borrow total rewards risk profile how risky where to play portfolio health funding fund the plan how is it funded launch risk starting position under-invested neglected self-funded harvest quadrant matrix growth share
body: BCG (growth vs RELATIVE share, Cipla divided by the leader) is the diagnosis. Cipla holds NO STAR and NO CASH COW anywhere in cardiac; its best relative share is 0.22 in A3. A4 0.018, A7 0.069, A3 0.220 and A1 0.041 are Question Marks (above-market growth, low relative share); A5 0.066, A8 0.162, A9 0.056 and A6 0.000 are Dogs. TWO CONSEQUENCES. First, A8 is a DOG, not a Cash Cow - which is exactly why 'harvest' was the wrong verb and CONVERT is right, and BCG reaches that on relative share alone, independently of our volume evidence. Second, with no cash cow in the book the plan CANNOT be funded by harvesting something healthy; it has to be funded by fixing a behaviour, which is what the conversion gap is. That is also the honest answer to why Cipla's cardiac book has been under-invested for years - nothing in it ever self-funded. ANSOFF is the description of the plan, and the numbers are exact. MARKET PENETRATION (existing brand, existing patient): Rs 68.1 Cr, 93% of the Rs 73.1 Cr gross - Cresar AMH 20.2, Rosulip-CV 16.2, Rosulip-ASP 15.4, Metolar Trio 10.0, Atorlip-CV 6.3. PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT (new molecule, same prescriber): Rs 5.0 Cr, 7% - the Horizon 2 triple. MARKET DEVELOPMENT (same brand, Tier-2/3 refill): zero incremental spend, served by the existing 5,500-stockist network. DIVERSIFICATION: deliberately empty; A4 would be in-licensed and sits outside the underwritten number. THE POINT: 93% of the plan sits in Ansoff's lowest-risk quadrant, and that was not chosen for comfort - Cipla ran seven cardiac launches in this window and made Rs 1.94 Cr between them, so the risk gradient Ansoff describes in theory is measured in this dataset. THE HR FRAMEWORKS are separate and sit in Annexure G: Build-Buy-Borrow for sourcing the 110 reps, Sales Force Effectiveness for whether 110 is the right number (8-12 calls/day benchmark; our panels compute to 9.1 and 11.4), and Total Rewards for cutting the incentive around conversion ratio rather than gross prescriptions. title: Why the cilnidipine triple, and why we changed our Round 1 answer

title: What our numbers assume, stated plainly
tags: assumption haircut take rate conservative limitation weakness confidence trust underwrite headroom benchmark
body: Three things a judge should hear from us before they find them. First, an earlier draft of this deck claimed prizes were sized after a 30% take-rate haircut. That was wrong: checking the model, no haircut was applied — A7's achievable share is exactly its ceiling, and Rs 69 Cr is the raw headroom. We removed the claim rather than defend it. Second, Rs 201 Cr is HEADROOM — what the pool structure permits, not a forecast. Reaching it needs a roughly 8.7x share move, and nobody starting where Cipla starts came close: across 279 companies over two years, the best multiple from a 0.2-2.0% base was 1.60x in A1 (Unison) and 1.90x in A7 (IPCA, 0.76 to 1.43%). So we UNDERWRITE Cipla matching the single best performer in each archetype, compounded to five years: Rs 38 Cr in A1 and Rs 35 Cr in A7, Rs 62 Cr net of cannibalisation — 31% of headroom, against a 16% break-even. Third, the ranking is re-run across 108 parameter combinations and A7 holds top-3 in all 108, so the call does not depend on the weights we chose.
source: Computed from the case dataset; benchmarks from all 279 companies, MAT24 to MAT26

body: 7,452 SKU records across 279 companies, MAT Feb'24 to Feb'26, with value, constant-price value and units. SUPERGROUP is CARDIAC throughout, but CARDIAC SEGMENT holds only three values: Anti-Hypertensives, Lipid Regulators, Anti Angina. That is why our market is ₹23,244 Cr while PharmaTrac's wider cardiovascular figure is ₹33,115 Cr (MAT Dec'25) — the difference is SGLT2i, ARNI, anticoagulants, beta-blockers and standalone diuretics, which this dataset excludes. We size on what we can see and say so.

title: How many Indians have hypertension — 315 million
tags: hypertension prevalence how many patients epidemiology burden india nfhs icmr indiab population tam 315 million total addressable
body: ICMR-INDIAB-17, the largest metabolic survey ever run in India (113,043 people, all 30 states and UTs, fieldwork 2008-2020, published in Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2023), puts hypertension prevalence at 35.5% of adults — an estimated 315 million people. Two earlier reference points, quoted only with their own age bands: NFHS-5 (2019-21) found 22.8% among adults aged 15-49, and ICMR-NNMS (2017-18) found 28.5% across 18-69. The three do not disagree; they measure different populations, and the spread is age structure. Use 315 million as the patient-universe figure and say which survey it comes from. NFHS-5 also found 52.1% of hypertension cases were NEWLY diagnosed at survey — over half the hypertensive population was unknown to the health system, which is the structural reason the treated pool keeps filling.
source: ICMR-INDIAB-17, Lancet Diab & Endo 2023; NFHS-5 (2019-21) IIPS/MoHFW; ICMR-NNMS 2017-18

title: The treatment cascade — and why it points at A7
tags: cascade treatment control uncontrolled resistant a7 triple why durable funnel diagnosed treated adherence nfhs
body: NFHS-5 measures the cascade among those already diagnosed: 40.7% were on BP-lowering medication, up from 32.6% in NFHS-4 — roughly 8 percentage points of treatment initiation in one survey cycle. Of those on medication, 73.7% had controlled BP, DOWN from 80.8% in NFHS-4. Read together: more patients are being started on therapy, and a growing share are not reaching target on what they are given. Patients on treatment but uncontrolled are definitionally the resistant-hypertension population — the A7 archetype. This is demand-side corroboration for A7 that does not come from the SKU file at all. Caveat to volunteer before being asked: NFHS control is a single-visit household measurement, not clinic-confirmed resistant hypertension, so this establishes direction and scale rather than a patient count.
source: NFHS-5 (2019-21) vs NFHS-4 (2015-16), IIPS/MoHFW

title: The metabolic cluster — diabetes, prediabetes and obesity
tags: diabetes prediabetes obesity metabolic cardiometabolic a3 comorbidity clustering indiab dysglycaemia
body: ICMR-INDIAB-17 national weighted prevalence, adults, 113,043 participants across all 30 states/UTs: diabetes 11.4%, prediabetes 15.3%, generalised obesity 28.6%, abdominal obesity 39.5%, hypertension 35.5%. Prediabetes exceeding diabetes is the forward indicator — that pool converts. All metabolic NCDs except prediabetes were more common in urban than rural areas, which matters for where a metro-first specialist force is deployed. This clustering is the epidemiological basis for the A3 cardiometabolic archetype: the same patient carries hypertension, dysglycaemia and dyslipidaemia, and is managed by one physician.
source: ICMR-INDIAB-17, Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2023

title: Dyslipidaemia prevalence — demand behind the lipid archetypes
tags: dyslipidaemia lipid cholesterol ldl hdl prevalence a1 a4 a5 statin screening indiab
body: ICMR-INDIAB-25 finds dyslipidaemia highly prevalent among Indian adults, especially at younger ages and among those with adverse glycaemic status, obesity or hypertension. The burden is driven predominantly by low HDL-C (66.8%). Two strategic consequences. First, a substantial share sits in people who are otherwise metabolically normal — the argument for broad lipid screening rather than screening only the obviously at-risk, and therefore for a larger statin and statin-combination pool than risk-based screening would suggest. Second, the clustering with hypertension and dysglycaemia underwrites both A3 and combination lipid therapy generally.
source: ICMR-INDIAB-25, Journal of Clinical Lipidology

title: Cardiovascular disease burden in India
tags: cvd cardiovascular deaths mortality burden gbd ischemic heart disease stroke why cardiac matters premature
body: CVD is the leading cause of death in India, accounting for roughly a quarter of all mortality. Ischaemic heart disease and stroke together cause more than 80% of CVD deaths. India's age-standardised CVD death rate is about 272 per 100,000 against a global average of 235 — a heavier burden than the world average, and striking at younger ages than in Western populations. This is the backdrop for why guideline bodies keep tightening targets (CSI 2024's crash-LDL thresholds, ESC's combination-first stance) and why cardiac is the therapy area Cipla is underweight in.
source: Global Burden of Disease / IHME; DCP-3 'Global Burden of Cardiovascular Disease in India'; WHO India

title: Cardiac is the largest therapy area in the Indian pharma market
tags: ipm indian pharmaceutical market size growth cardiac share therapy area largest pharmatrac chronic 2026 sector
body: PharmaTrac (Pharmarack) 2026 figures: the Indian Pharmaceutical Market stands at roughly ₹2.44 lakh crore on a MAT basis, growing about 8.4% in value while unit growth stays near 0.7% — the market is growing on price and mix, not volume. Against that backdrop cardiac stands out: it is the LARGEST single therapy area at 14-15% of IPM value, and it grew 13.2-14.3% through early 2026, roughly 1.7 times the market. May 2026 cardiac sales were about ₹3,184 crore in the month. Chronic and sub-chronic segments together hold 57% of IPM. Two things follow: cardiac is not a niche Cipla would be entering, it is the biggest room in the house; and it is one of the few therapy areas growing on real demand rather than price.
source: PharmaTrac / Pharmarack, Jan-May 2026 monthly IPM reports

title: IHCI — the government programme that shapes A7 demand
tags: ihci india hypertension control initiative programme government districts scale public health protocol
body: The India Hypertension Control Initiative began in 2018-19 across 26 districts in five states and has scaled to 141 districts across 25 states, covering about 303 million people through 21,579 health facilities. Of roughly 1.24 million hypertensives enrolled across 15 states, about 1.05 million remained under care. BP control among those under care runs around 43-44%, and in the nine longest running districts improved from 37% to 48% between 2018-19 and 2023-24. IHCI is the reason the Step-3 telmisartan-backbone triple is a protocol standard rather than a commercial invention — which is exactly what insulates it from CDSCO's irrational-FDC bans.
source: IHCI outcome papers, BMC Health Services Research 2024; Resolve to Save Lives; ihci.in

title: THE COUNTERARGUMENT: public supply is displacing private purchase
tags: risk threat out of pocket public procurement free medicines government displacement counterargument weakness against thesis jan aushadhi
body: THIS CUTS AGAINST OUR THESIS AND WE SHOULD RAISE IT BEFORE A JUDGE DOES. In IHCI districts the proportion of patients PAYING for their hypertension medicines fell from 47% to 9%. Those patients did not stop taking medicine — they moved from the private retail market, which is what the case dataset measures, to free public supply, which it does not. IHCI now covers 303 million people. Alongside it, 16,912 Jan Aushadhi Kendras were operating as of June 2025, and the scheme claims roughly ₹38,000 crore of cumulative savings to citizens through generic pricing. Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY covers about 55 crore people in 12.37 crore families at ₹5 lakh per family per year. The honest read: the private branded-generic pool a Cipla triple competes in is being squeezed from below in exactly the Tier 2-3 geographies where the stockist network is Cipla's advantage. That argues for a metro and Tier-1 specialist-led entry, which is what our persona sizing already concluded — but for a different reason than we originally gave.
source: IHCI outcome papers; PMBJP/Jan Aushadhi as of 30 Jun 2025; NHA PM-JAY programme data

title: Where the patients are — hypertension by state
tags: state states geography where launch metro city region prevalence punjab kerala telangana delhi rollout sequence which cities pilot four metros
body: NFHS-5 age-standardised hypertension prevalence varies roughly two-fold across India. Highest: Sikkim (34.5% women / 41.6% men, ~32.2% overall), Punjab (31.2% / 37.7%), with Kerala, West Bengal and Telangana also in the upper band. Lowest: Rajasthan (15.4% / 17.9%) and Ladakh (15.7% / 17.4%). Burden concentrates in southern and eastern states. Among the over-60s specifically — the population most likely to be uncontrolled on two agents, i.e. the A7 patient — prevalence is highest in Delhi, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Punjab, Sikkim and Telangana. Note the north-eastern states show high prevalence in the UNDER-30s, a different and smaller commercial opportunity despite the headline rate.
source: NFHS-5 (2019-21), IIPS/MoHFW; district-level analysis, medRxiv 2023

title: OUR SYNTHESIS: prevalence alone is the wrong launch criterion
tags: launch geography where first four metros top 30 cities sequence rollout which states avoid kerala jan aushadhi payer mix tension our synthesis
body: THIS IS OUR INFERENCE FROM TWO PUBLIC SOURCES, NOT A PUBLISHED FINDING — present it as reasoning, not as a citation. Naive logic says launch where prevalence is highest, which points at Kerala, Punjab, Telangana and West Bengal. But the southern states leading on prevalence are the same ones leading on Jan Aushadhi density: Kerala has 1,525 kendras, Karnataka 1,417 and Tamil Nadu 1,357, the three highest in India. High prevalence and high generic-displacement pressure sit in the same postcodes, and a branded triple competes worst exactly there. The defensible criterion is prevalence AND private-payer depth AND specialist density together — which points at Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Punjab's urban belt (Ludhiana, Chandigarh) and Hyderabad: high elderly hypertension burden, concentrated private cardiology, and comparatively lower public-supply substitution. Kerala is the trap: the best epidemiology and the worst payer mix for what we are selling.
source: Synthesis of NFHS-5 state prevalence and PMBJP state-wise kendra counts (Jun 2025)

title: Why the volume growth should persist — the outside view
tags: durable growth volume sustainable outlook will it continue forecast confidence outside view corroboration three reasons
body: The case dataset shows A7 growing 16.8% with 11.2 points of that from volume. Whether that persists is the question a strategy audience actually asks, and four independent public sources point the same way. One: 52.1% of hypertension cases in NFHS-5 were newly diagnosed, so the diagnosed pool is still filling from a universe of about 315 million (ICMR-INDIAB). Two: treatment initiation among the diagnosed rose from 32.6% to 40.7% in one survey cycle. Three: BP control among the treated FELL from 80.8% to 73.7%, so the uncontrolled-on-therapy pool — what a triple addresses — grows from both ends at once. Four: cardiac is the largest IPM therapy area at 14-15% share and grew about 14% in 2026, against 8.4% for the market. None of these come from the case dataset. The one caution: see `ihci-risk` — part of that expanding treated pool is being served by free public supply rather than private retail.
source: NFHS-4/NFHS-5 IIPS-MoHFW; ICMR-INDIAB-17 Lancet 2023; PharmaTrac 2026
